meta.title: Is "When God closes a door, He opens a window" in the Bible? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in the Bible — but not from The Sound of Music either. It was quoted in American newspapers as an Italian proverb from 1901, sixty-four years before the film.
meta.ogTitle: Is 'When God closes a door, He opens a window' in the Bible?
meta.ogDescription: Both common answers are wrong. It is not scripture, and the film did not coin it: American newspapers quoted it as an Italian proverb from 1901.

answer.label: Not scripture — an Italian proverb, in English by 1901
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · quoted as an Italian proverb from 1901
answer.sourceLine: It appears in no book of the Bible — a point made plainly by Christian sources themselves. But it is not a Sound of Music invention either, which is what most corrections claim. It was circulating in American newspapers as a quoted Italian proverb by 1901, sixty-four years before the film: ‘When God shuts a door He opens a window.’ The film popularised it; it did not coin it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: No — appears in no book of the Bible

1965 — spoken by the Mother Abbess, not Maria

source.excerpt: The Italians have an old saying that "when God closes a door he opens a window".
trail: Christian sources say plainly that it is not in the Bible — The Gospel Coalition calls it one of several ‘biblical-sounding phrases’ that are not scripture The Gospel Coalition ↗, and John MacArthur’s ministry files it as a cliché Grace to You ↗.

The usual correction stops there and credits The Sound of Music. That is wrong. Searching digitised American newspapers turns it up as a quoted Italian proverb from 11 April 1901 (New Haven), again in 1903, and as a syndicated filler item in the New-York Tribune in 1906 Library of Congress, 1903 ↗.

The film wording differs and belongs to the Mother Abbess, not Maria: ‘When the Lord closes a door… somewhere He opens a window.’ Maria later repeats it back, quoting her — which is probably why she gets the credit Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: The earliest instance we located using the verb ‘closes’. Note what the newspaper does: it presents the line as somebody else’s proverb, already old. That is the shape of a saying in circulation, not one being coined.
source.rightsNote: Free to reuse. The saying was in print in American newspapers from 1901 and was already being quoted as an older Italian proverb, so the words themselves are long out of copyright — you may reproduce them commercially. Two cautions: the specific 1965 film wording (‘When the Lord closes a door… somewhere He opens a window’) is screenplay text and still protected, so quote the proverb rather than the film line; and the Italian original usually given, Quando Dio chiude una porta, apre una finestra, is not something we could date to a scholarly source, so we do not present it as the attested original. This is not legal advice.

author.name: The Bible
author.heading: Why people think it is scripture
author.metaLine: The collected scriptures of Judaism and Christianity · commonly credited here in error
author.bio: The Bible attracts this kind of adoption because so much of English moral vocabulary genuinely came from it, and readers reasonably assume that a saying which sounds scriptural probably is. It is far from alone in being wrongly credited: ‘God helps those who help themselves’, ‘cleanliness is next to godliness’ and ‘money is the root of all evil’ are all outside it, misremembered, or both. Nothing here bears on what scripture says or on anyone’s faith; the question on this page is narrow — where a particular English sentence came from — and the answer is an anonymous Italian proverb that circulated in American newspapers decades before the 1965 film.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Two answers circulate and both are wrong. It is not in the Bible — that much the usual corrections get right. But those same corrections then credit a 1965 film, and the saying is older than that by more than sixty years.

items.why: It appears in no book of the Bible. Christian sources say so directly rather than defending it The Gospel Coalition ↗.
The standard debunk credits the 1965 film. But the saying is in American newspapers from 1901, always as somebody else’s proverb. The film spread it; it did not invent it.

items.scope: Who says it in the film
items.why: The line is the Mother Abbess’s. Maria repeats it later, explicitly quoting her — and gets the credit because hers is the version audiences remember.
Every 1901–1916 instance calls it Italian, but we could not date the Italian text to a scholarly source, so we do not print it as the attested original.
The secular version — no God, no window — is a distinct family with its own disputed credits to Alexander Graham Bell and Helen Keller. Do not treat instances of one as evidence for the other.

misattribution.truthLine: Not in the Bible, and not from the film. An anonymous saying quoted as an Italian proverb in American newspapers from 1901 the 1903 printing ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the sentence people reach for when consoling someone, and its power comes from sounding scriptural without committing to any doctrine. That is also why it is so often challenged — it promises a compensating window that no scripture actually guarantees.

The more interesting finding is how confidently the correction is wrong. ‘It’s from The Sound of Music’ has become the standard debunk, repeated by sources that checked the Bible carefully and then stopped looking. The proverb was consoling American newspaper readers when Rodgers and Hammerstein were children.
detailsBody: 11 April 1901, New Haven: ‘the beautiful Italian proverb: When God shuts a door He opens a window.’
27 August 1903, Minnesota: the earliest ‘closes’ wording — ‘The Italians have an old saying…’
1 May 1906, New-York Tribune: a syndicated filler item carries it nationally.
1908 and 1916: still circulating, still labelled Italian.
1965: the film gives it the wording most people now recite — sixty-four years after it first appeared in English.
context.pull: The standard debunk credits a 1965 film. The proverb is from 1901.
